name: Westinghouse iGen4500
summary: The sweet spot for a home that has outgrown a 2,200W suitcase unit but does not want an open-frame engine droning all night.
verdict: The iGen4500 fills the gap many outage shoppers land in: more load than a small inverter can handle, but not the budget or patience for a 9,000-watt open frame. Westinghouse rates it at 3,700 running and 4,500 starting watts, which handles a refrigerator, a freezer, a gas furnace blower, a sump pump, lights and electronics as long as you are sensible about what runs at the same time. As an inverter, it makes power clean enough for sensitive electronics, and its engine throttles back at light load, which is where the long run time on a 3.4-gallon tank comes from. Owners commonly report it is clearly quieter than open-frame units of similar output, and remote start is a real comfort in a February storm. The limit is the 120V-only panel, which rules out a 240V well pump or an electric range. Expect roughly $1,000 to $1,300 at the time of writing.

name: Honda EU2200i
summary: The best small generator you can buy for keeping food cold, phones charged and a few lights on.
verdict: The EU2200i is the small inverter others are measured against, and the reasons are mostly unglamorous: it starts, it keeps starting, and dealer support for Honda engines is everywhere. Its ratings are 1,800 running and 2,200 starting watts, enough for a refrigerator plus lights, internet, phone charging and a TV, or a gas furnace blower by itself. Honda lists run time at about 3.2 hours at full rated load and about 8.1 hours at a quarter load on the 0.95-gallon tank, so build your fuel supply around those figures. Noise is rated at 48 to 57 dBA, which is why owners say they can run it near a neighbor's bedroom window without complaints. CO-MINDER stops the engine if carbon monoxide gathers nearby, a backup to good placement rather than a replacement for it. Two EU2200i units can be paralleled for more output. Expect roughly $1,100 to $1,300 at the time of writing.

name: Champion 2500-Watt Ultralight Inverter
summary: Best value among small inverters when light weight and a lower price matter more than the brand name.
verdict: For well under the Honda's price, Champion's ultralight 2500-watt inverter covers most of the same ground. Its rating of 1,850 running and 2,500 starting watts gives it slightly more surge headroom than the EU2200i for refrigerator and small pump starts. At around 39 pounds, it is the easiest unit on this list to carry up basement steps or lift into a truck bed. Champion lists up to roughly 8 hours at a quarter load on its small tank, which is enough to keep a refrigerator going overnight as long as little else is plugged in. The CO Shield system cuts the engine when carbon monoxide builds up nearby, and a second Champion inverter can be paralleled with it for more output. Owners commonly describe it as easy to start and pleasantly quiet, with the standard small-engine caveat that monthly runs and stabilized fuel keep it that way. At the time of writing it sells for roughly $500 to $700.

name: Generac GP3500iO Open-Frame Inverter
summary: The sensible step up when 2,000 watts falls short but the iGen4500 costs more than you want to pay.
verdict: The GP3500iO sits between the suitcase inverters and full-size portables. Generac rates it at 3,000 running and 3,500 starting watts, and its PowerRUSH feature is built to help start motor loads, such as a sump pump or a window air conditioner, that a 2,200-watt unit can struggle with. That makes it a reasonable small-house choice for a refrigerator, freezer, sump pump and lights together, provided the start-ups are staggered. Because it is an inverter, the output is clean for electronics, and it throttles down at light loads to save fuel. The open frame keeps the price and weight below an enclosed design, but it also lets more engine noise escape, so it is a poor fit for a narrow side yard beside a neighbor's bedroom. COsense shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide accumulates. At the time of writing it sells for roughly $650 to $900.

name: Firman W01784 Compact Inverter
summary: A low-cost inverter for lights, electronics or a refrigerator on its own, not a full essentials load.
verdict: The Firman W01784 is the cheapest way into inverter power on this list. It belongs to the 2,000-watt peak class, and its running output, roughly 1,600 to 1,700 watts depending on the listing, falls somewhat below the Honda and Champion. That handles a modern refrigerator by itself, or lights, a modem, a TV and phone and laptop charging together, but it leaves little margin to pair the fridge with much else. It is compact and light enough to keep in a closet, and its inverter output is safe for electronics. The low price is paid for in margin: less output, a thinner service network and a shorter long-term reliability record than Honda or Champion. For a townhouse near apartment scale, a camper, or a household that mostly wants the fridge and internet running, it is a sensible purchase. At the time of writing it sells for roughly $400 to $550.

name: Honda EU7000iS Inverter Generator
summary: The pick when noise matters and the pump is 3/4 HP or smaller, or 1 HP started on its own.
verdict: Most quiet inverter generators are 120-volt only and cannot run a 240V well pump at all. The Honda EU7000iS is one of the exceptions: Honda rates it at 7,000 starting and 5,500 running watts with a 120/240V, 30-amp locking outlet, in an enclosed, fuel-injected package that is far quieter than the open-frame units on this list. That makes it the best choice for close neighbors or anyone who will run the generator for days. The trade-off is headroom. A 1/2 or 3/4 HP pump is well within its capability, but a 1 HP pump is near the top of what the starting rating comfortably covers, so let the pump start with other motor loads off, and check your motor maker's sizing table before relying on it for anything larger. It also costs substantially more per watt than the open-frame options; you are paying for quiet, clean output and Honda's long service record.

name: Westinghouse iGen4500DF Dual Fuel Inverter Generator
summary: The quiet, fuel-efficient dual fuel choice for essentials and RV duty, not for wiring into a panel.
verdict: If you want dual fuel without the noise of an open-frame engine, the iGen4500DF is the one to look at. Westinghouse rates it at 3,700 running and 4,500 peak watts on gasoline, and 3,330 running and 4,050 peak on propane. Because it is an inverter, the engine throttles down at light load, which is why the spec sheet lists 18 hours at quarter load on its 3.4-gallon tank and 14 hours on a standard 20 lb propane cylinder. That is the best propane economy on this list by a wide margin. Output is clean, with Westinghouse listing under 3 percent total harmonic distortion, and the operating noise is rated as low as 52 dBA. The limits are important. It is 120V only, with a 5-20R duplex, a TT-30R RV outlet and two USB ports, and Westinghouse's own sheet marks it as not transfer switch ready. So it is a run-extension-cords-to-essentials generator, or an RV generator, not a panel-feeding one. It weighs 98 lb dry. It can be paralleled with another iGen using Westinghouse's cord if you outgrow one.

name: WEN 56380i Super Quiet 3800-Watt Portable Inverter Generator with Electric Start
summary: The budget way to get mid-size inverter output with a push-button start.
verdict: WEN has built a large following by selling inverter generators with mid-size output at prices well below the big names, and the 56380i is its sweet spot. WEN rates it at 3,400 running and 3,800 surge watts from a 212cc OHV engine, which covers a refrigerator, a freezer, lights, internet and a furnace blower with some staggering. WEN lists noise at 57 dBA at quarter load and run time of up to 8.5 hours at half load. Electric start with a recoil backup is unusual at this price, and the fuel shutoff valve lets you run the carburetor dry before storage, which is the single best habit for a generator that sits most of the year. It is compatible with WEN's 56421 parallel kit. The trade-offs are real. WEN's published specs do not list a carbon monoxide shutoff, so placement and indoor CO alarms carry all the safety weight. At 99.2 lb it is as heavy as the Westinghouse iGen4500 with less output, and WEN's service network is thinner than Honda's or Generac's. For a buyer who wants push-button convenience and 3,000-plus watts on a budget, it is a sensible pick.

name: Honda EU3200i Inverter Generator with CO-MINDER
summary: The Honda to buy if the EU2200i is just short of what your refrigerator, freezer and furnace need together.
verdict: The EU3200i is Honda's answer to buyers who love the EU2200i but keep bumping into its 1,800-watt ceiling. Retail spec listings rate it at 3,200 maximum and 2,600 running watts from a Honda GX130 engine, roughly 44 percent more continuous output than the EU2200i in a package that still weighs only about 59 lb dry. That extra margin is what lets a refrigerator, a chest freezer and a gas furnace blower run together without tripping the overload light every time two compressors start at once. Noise is listed at 54 dBA at quarter load and 58 dBA at rated load, very close to the smaller Honda. Run time is about 3.3 hours at rated load and 8.6 hours at quarter load on a 1.2-gallon tank. CO-MINDER shuts the generator down if carbon monoxide builds to unsafe levels around it. Two units can be paralleled for up to 6,400 watts with Honda's kit. The downsides are price and the recoil-only start. If you can live with 1,800 watts, the EU2200i is better value; if you cannot, this is the quiet, carryable step up.

name: Yamaha EF2200iS Inverter Generator
summary: The premium alternative to the Honda for buyers who value run time per tank and a fuel gauge.
verdict: Yamaha's EF2200iS is the closest thing the Honda EU2200i has to a direct rival, and on a couple of points it wins. Yamaha rates it at 2,200 maximum and 1,800 rated watts, the same as the Honda, but its 1.24-gallon tank gives up to 10.5 hours at quarter load, a meaningful edge for overnight refrigerator duty. It also has a fuel gauge, which sounds trivial until you are checking a tank by flashlight in the rain. Yamaha lists noise at 57 dBA at quarter load and 65 dBA at rated load, measured at 7 meters, so it is a little louder than the Honda when working hard. Dry weight is 55.2 lb, about 8 lb more than the EU2200i, still a one-person carry. Two units can be paralleled with Yamaha's Twin Tech cable for 30 amps of rated output. Some recent listings describe a version with a CO sensor, so check the listing if carbon monoxide shutoff matters to you, and it should. Price lands close to the Honda; choose the Yamaha if run time and the gauge matter more to you than Honda's larger service network.

name: Champion 4500-Watt Electric Start Dual Fuel Inverter Generator with CO Shield (201319)
summary: The dual fuel inverter to buy for most homes and RVs: enough propane watts for essentials, CO shutoff and a noise rating with a stated distance.
verdict: The 201319 earns the top spot by doing everything a dual fuel inverter needs to do without a weak spot. Champion rates it at 3,500 running watts on gasoline and 3,150 on propane, with 4,500 starting watts on either fuel, which matters when a refrigerator compressor or a sump pump kicks on. The 61 dBA rating is measured at 23 feet, one of the few noise figures on this list with a stated distance. On a 20 lb cylinder Champion lists up to 21 hours at a quarter load, and 14 hours on the 2.25-gallon gasoline tank. The panel has a TT-30R for a 30-amp RV, a 5-20R household duplex and a 12V outlet, and CO Shield shuts the engine off if carbon monoxide builds up around it. Start is electric with a pull cord as backup, and the warranty is three years. The limits: it is 120V only, so it cannot feed a 240V panel or well pump, and the gas tank is small. Champion also sells the 201321 open-frame version, rated at 3,650 / 3,285 running watts, 64 dBA and 92.6 lb.

name: Generac iQ5200DF Dual Fuel Inverter Generator with COsense
summary: The pick when 3,150 propane watts feel tight: more power on propane, long half-load run time and CO shutoff.
verdict: The iQ5200DF is the pick when the Champion's 3,150 propane watts feel tight. Generac rates it at 3,900 running and 5,200 starting watts on gasoline and 3,500 running and 4,700 starting on propane, from a 223cc engine with push-button electric start and a pull-cord backup. Run time is its strongest spec: Generac lists 11 hours at half load and 20 hours at a quarter load on a 20 lb cylinder, and 9 and 15 hours on the 3.2-gallon gasoline tank. COsense shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide builds up, and the panel carries two GFCI 5-20R outlets, a 120V 30-amp L5-30R locking outlet and USB-A and USB-C ports. It is parallel ready with Generac's kit #7668. Two caveats: Generac publishes no dBA figure, and its own sources list the weight as 111 lb on the product page and 107 lb on the spec sheet. One owner review on Lowe's describes a unit that would not run on propane, which Generac replaced, so run any new generator on propane once at home rather than for the first time in an outage.

Its 22-hour quarter-load run time on a 20 lb cylinder is the longest listed among the mid-size picks, and the 3.4-gallon gas tank is rated for 18 hours at the same load. summary: The dual fuel inverter for running house circuits through a transfer switch, including a 240V well pump.
verdict: This is the dual fuel inverter for people who want to run house circuits rather than extension cords. Champion rates the 201417 at 9,000 running watts on gasoline and 8,100 on propane, with 11,000 starting watts on both fuels, enough to start a 240V well pump or a central air compressor that a 120V inverter cannot touch. summary: The best choice if your house has natural gas service and you want a portable that never needs refueling.
verdict: If your house has a natural gas meter, this tri fuel inverter can run from the utility line for as long as the gas keeps flowing. Westinghouse rates it at 9,000 running watts on gasoline, 8,100 on propane and 7,200 on natural gas, with peaks of 12,000, 11,000 and 9,800. It is 120/240V with an L14-30R, a 14-50R and a GFCI 5-20R duplex, and Westinghouse lists it as transfer switch ready. A CO sensor is standard, and start is electric, remote or recoil. Noise is rated as low as 64 dBA, and dry weight is 191 lb. Naming is in flux: Westinghouse's iGen11000TFc page now displays this model as the iGen12000TFc, with the same running ratings and higher peaks, and retailers still list both. If you have no gas line, the dual fuel iGen12000DFc carries the same gasoline and propane ratings.

name: Honda EU3000iS Inverter Generator
summary: The safest single-generator choice for a 30-amp trailer with one rooftop AC, if you can afford it and move it.
verdict: The EU3000iS is the generator many experienced RVers end up with after trying cheaper ones. Honda rates it at 3,000 watts maximum and 2,800 watts rated, which is enough to start and run most 13,500 BTU rooftop air conditioners along with the converter and fridge, and its TT-30R outlet means a 30-amp rig plugs in directly. Electric start makes it easy to fire up from a seat, and Honda's CO-MINDER system shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide builds up around it. The 3.4-gallon tank lets it run through a long day at moderate load, and the enclosed design keeps it quiet enough for most campgrounds. The catch is weight. At around 130 pounds, it lives on its wheels and needs a ramp or a carrier to get into a truck. If your rooftop unit is a 15,000 BTU model, add a soft starter or look one size up.

verdict: The iGen4500DFc takes the popular iGen4500 platform and adds dual fuel and a CO sensor, which is what the c at the end of the model name signals. Westinghouse rates it at 4,500 peak and 3,700 running watts on gasoline, comfortably above the 3,600 watts a TT-30R outlet can deliver. That surplus is the point. On a hot day or at altitude, when engine output falls, it still has enough left to start a 15,000 BTU rooftop unit and keep the converter and fridge running. Remote start lets you fire it from inside the rig, and the propane option means you can run from the tanks you already carry. Westinghouse markets it as a quiet unit at light load, and it is parallel capable if you ever outgrow it. Expect lower output on propane, and plan for its weight and size when you think about where it rides.

summary: More generator for less money than the premium brands, with the propane flexibility RVers want.
verdict: Champion's 4500-watt dual fuel inverter is one of the most common generators you will see parked beside travel trailers, and for good reason. Champion rates it at 4,500 starting and 3,700 running watts on gasoline, which covers a 15,000 BTU rooftop air conditioner plus everyday loads, and the dual fuel system lets you run it off a spare 20-pound cylinder instead of hauling gas cans. The TT-30R outlet plugs a 30-amp rig in directly, and electric start avoids the pull cord. It is parallel capable with compatible Champion inverters, and Champion has a broad service network and a reputation for answering the phone. The trade-offs are the usual ones for this class: it is heavy enough to need its wheels, it is a little louder than a Honda when working hard, and it makes less power on propane. For buyers who want headroom without paying Honda money, it is the default choice.

name: Champion 3400-Watt Dual Fuel Inverter Generator
summary: The budget answer for a 30-amp trailer with a 13,500 BTU AC, ideally paired with a soft starter.
verdict: The Champion 3400 is the generator that made dual fuel inverters affordable for weekend RVers. Champion rates it at 3,400 starting and 3,100 running watts on gasoline, which puts a 13,500 BTU rooftop air conditioner within reach for many rigs, especially with a soft starter fitted. It has a TT-30R outlet, electric start on most versions, and the ability to run on propane from your RV tanks, so you can leave the gas can at home. Champion builds parallel capability in, so a second inverter can be added later. Where it falls short is headroom. A 15,000 BTU unit, a hot afternoon or a campground at elevation can push it to its limit, and when it works hard, it gets louder. It is also heavy for its output. Buy it for a mid-size trailer with one 13,500 BTU AC, not for a big rig with every appliance running.

name: Honda EU1000i Inverter Generator
summary: The generator for campers who never cook electrically and want something they barely notice carrying.
verdict: The EU1000i is the generator for campers who have done the math and found they do not need 2,000 watts. Honda rates it at 1,000 watts maximum and 900 rated, which is plenty for phones, laptops, lights, fans, a 12-volt fridge and recharging a power station, but not enough for an electric kettle, a coffee maker or an induction burner. At about 29 pounds, it is light enough to carry to a walk-in site or tuck into a crowded trunk, and it is quiet at the light loads a campsite actually presents. It pairs especially well with a 1kWh power station: the battery covers the night and any short high-power bursts, while the Honda recharges it during generator hours. It is expensive for its output, and you will outgrow it if you take up a trailer, but if lightness and quiet are what you value most, nothing else on this list comes close.

name: WEN 56203i Inverter Generator
summary: A good-value inverter for a few camping trips a year, not a decade of heavy use.
verdict: The WEN 56203i is the generator to buy when the budget is tight but you still want a real inverter rather than a loud open-frame unit. WEN rates it at 2,000 surge and 1,600 rated watts, which covers charging, lights, a fan, a small TV and most 1,500-watt-or-smaller heating appliances if you run them alone. WEN quotes 51 dBA at quarter load, in the same quiet class as the premium picks, and at about 39 pounds it is easy to carry. Eco mode throttles the engine down when you are only charging devices, and the inverter output is clean enough for laptops and phones. The trade-offs are durability and support. It is not built to the same standard as the Honda or Yamaha, and service options are thinner. For campers who go out a handful of times a year and maintain it properly, it does the job for well under half the price of the premium brands.

name: Generac GP2500i Inverter Generator
summary: The small inverter for campers who run kettles, hot plates or heaters for long stretches.
verdict: Generac's GP2500i is the small inverter for campers who lean on heating loads. Generac rates it at 2,500 starting and 2,200 running watts, the highest continuous output among the compact picks, which gives real margin when a 1,500-watt kettle or hot plate runs alongside charging loads, or when you want to run a heating appliance for an extended stretch without pushing the generator to its limit. Economy mode drops engine speed at light loads, and it can be paralleled with a second compatible Generac for more power. Generac's dealer network is broad, which helps when parts are needed. It is a little heavier than the WEN and Champion, still manageable for one person, and like any small inverter it gets louder at full load. Choose it if you cook electrically every day of the trip; if you mostly charge devices, the extra running watts do little for you.
